name: Yusuf Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. Tell me about your normal machine shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Yusuf, 58, and I feed printed board through a die cutter that makes folding cartons. I hold a vocational machine-operations certificate and have run this line for nine years; I know the usual jams, but the engineer handles serious electrical faults. A carton with a ragged fold is waste even if the shift screen calls it a good run.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like financially, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Rina does catering shifts, and our grown sons live elsewhere. My operator rate is low, her hours come and go, we have about three weeks of expenses saved, and there are only a couple of similar factories close enough to commute to. I use AI every day to find manual sections and compare plain-language fault notes, then check the press and the written safety sheet myself. I am keen to learn new controls early, and I support union rules that make practical training paid and available to the night crew. Retirement sounds attractive, but no income figure has yet cleared our actual bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the carton crew that the new office forecasting may stop us running out of board, which would help. I would still inspect the first fold after every die change; a forecast cannot feel a blunt edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The machine work stays for now, but three weeks saved and a low rate mean I watch each roster closely. Rina's catering shifts are irregular. I use AI daily, yet an office improvement is not a raise for operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the board feed and checking the first folded carton with the engineer after die changes. I would use my existing AI manual search for fault notes, then test against the safety sheet. At this month's union safety meeting I would ask for the forecast's proposed shift and staffing changes in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our usual thin margin, not about the office screen itself. A missing shift costs more than a missed forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you spot the blunt edge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A ragged fibre line shows up along the fold, and the next carton starts tearing at the corner. I stop the feed and ask the engineer to check the die before a whole pallet is spoiled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for staffing changes now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plant once moved a board delivery and left us short of a second person for unloading. I want the union safety meeting to ask for the actual roster, even if management says the new system is only in the office.

say: Office **board forecasts** may help, but first folds still need inspection.
I would ask the **union meeting** for any real staffing change in writing.
think: Three weeks of **savings** leave little cover for a missed shift.
Daily **AI manual searches** do not raise my lower operator rate.
do: **Keep** setting board feed and inspecting the first fold.
**Check** daily AI fault searches against the written machine safety sheet.
**Raise** the roster and staffing question at this month's union safety meeting.
feel: **Anxious** because ordinary roster losses would hurt our thin household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say an AI board schedule may reduce idle time, but a robot hand is still three years away from clearing our cutter. I would volunteer for a guarded camera trial if they pay us for it and show the actual roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like testing things. A tighter schedule can turn two short shifts into one and cut my already low wages. Rina cannot promise catering hours to fill that gap. The camera might catch a crooked print, but it must not become an excuse to remove the spotter without proving it safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request the proposed roster and a paid guarded trial on waste board. If the offer comes, I would learn the new AI print-alignment screen by marking deliberately skewed cartons and comparing its flags with a ruler beside the engineer. I would take the trial result to the scheduled union safety meeting; if paid shifts actually drop, I would apply only to posted safe local machine roles whose guaranteed pay after travel and shift times meet our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about fewer paid hours. Testing a tool is exciting; a test does not cover groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would measure an offset print at both edges of a scrap carton, then compare my ruler with the camera's alert. The engineer must keep the guard closed and stop the line for any adjustment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave for the first job advert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. There are few similar local jobs, and an advertised rate might depend on overtime. I need the actual base wage and journey cost before I give up a paid shift.

say: I would accept a **paid guarded trial** if the cutter camera is offered.
The plant should post **actual shifts** before relying on a tighter schedule.
think: A merged **short-shift roster** could cut an already low wage.
Rina's **irregular catering** cannot reliably cover missing hours.
do: **Request** the proposed roster and an offered paid guarded scrap trial.
**Learn** the new AI alignment screen only during supervised marked-carton practice.
**Apply** after actual cuts to posted safe local jobs at bill-covering net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic paid-hour loss despite curiosity about the camera.

fieldNote: His **AI learning** is new camera-control practice on guarded waste board, distinct from daily searches of manuals.
A **job application** would follow real hour cuts and posted safe work with a viable guaranteed wage after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the cutter team AGI may plan carton orders in 2028, while capable robots that feed board and clear the die arrive around 2031. I want the employer and union to negotiate paid transition posts before the robot line is commissioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when the physical work can be automated. I expect our cutter shifts to disappear, and three weeks of savings will be gone almost at once if Rina's catering is also quiet. I have started waking before dawn over whether rent or food would come first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would cancel our planned trip to see our sons and keep that cash for bills. I would attend the scheduled union bargaining meeting to press for paid release and safe practical places. I would enrol in a recognised tooling-maintenance course only if it is accepted by nearby plants, funded, paid during release and taught with supervised lockout on a guarded cutter. After qualifying and losing shifts, I would apply to posted safe local maintenance roles only if base pay after travel and shift times covers costs; without a course place, I would apply to posted safe packing-machine roles on the same terms while keeping any paid cutter shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A clever manual search cannot replace a cutter wage after the line shuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why tooling maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already know when a die edge is going dull, but I do not hold the maintenance credential. A real course should teach me to isolate the cutter, replace a die safely and check a test fold under a trainer's eye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop working at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written retirement income plus Rina's dependable earnings cover rent, food, travel and health costs. We have not established that; I cannot put an imagined payment into the budget.

say: I would distinguish **2028 order AGI** from physical cutter robots around 2031.
The **union negotiation** should secure paid transition posts before commissioning.
think: At **63**, I expect the physical cutter shifts to disappear.
Three weeks of **savings** cannot absorb a long income gap.
do: **Cancel** the sons' visit and hold the travel money for bills.
**Attend** the scheduled union bargaining meeting for paid safe training.
**Enrol** only in funded paid recognised guarded maintenance, then apply to posted jobs at viable pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and waking early over bills.
S2.quote: A clever manual search cannot replace a cutter wage after the line shuts.
fieldNote: He expects **2031 physical robots** to threaten the die cutter after 2028 AGI first affects order planning.
His **maintenance and packing** applications depend on real safe local postings with guaranteed net wages and shifts that cover costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union committee that AGI might plan carton orders in 2031, while capable robots handle board around 2034. Five years is useful if a nearby plant will actually accept a tooling credential and fund hands-on learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 then. I enjoy new technology, but our three-week reserve and low pay make an unfunded course a gamble I cannot take. We might retire before 2034 only if written income covers costs; until we run those numbers, a job matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union committee at its next meeting to seek paid places and written robot staffing dates. I would ask the two nearby plants which tooling qualification their posted jobs require; if an accepted funded course with paid release and supervised guarded lockout is offered, I would enrol. After passing and losing shifts, I would apply for posted safe local maintenance only if guaranteed wages after travel and shifts cover bills; if no real place opens, I would search posted safe packing-machine jobs on the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about being priced out of a useful course. With five years I could learn a machine, but I cannot work for free while I learn machine maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove another plant accepts the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the exact certificate name with a current local vacancy, then ask the hiring manager whether the guarded practice counts. A generic online badge would not be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you prepare at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the cutter running safely, and I would use my usual AI searches to find the manufacturer manual section for each fault. Those searches are already part of my shift, not the new qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the shop that AGI may plan cartons in 2036, with capable robots handling the actual cutter around 2039. Ten years gives me time to see retirement figures, though it does not give us ten years of wages in advance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 at the robot date if I still have a shift. I would like to retire earlier, but only if written income and Rina's dependable work cover rent, food and health needs; right now three weeks saved makes that doubtful. Daily AI use and willingness to train do not erase the need for a paid job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking safe paid cutter shifts and request written retirement-income estimates against a household cost list this year. I would ask the union at its next meeting for accepted funded tooling courses with paid release and supervised guarded lockout; if a real place is offered, I would enrol. If I remain at work after 2036 and shifts shrink, I would apply only to posted safe local machine or maintenance jobs whose base wage after travel and shift times covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the retirement arithmetic, even with the robot date far away. Time is useful only if there is something paid to do with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you actually leave paid work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rina and I would compare written retirement income with housing, food, transport and likely health costs. If those figures cover us reliably, I would leave earlier than a robot forced me to; if they do not, I would keep seeking paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is offered only online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current paid shift and ask for a practical place. I need a trainer beside a guarded isolated cutter before I can claim to maintain one safely.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 AGI picture is hardest because capable robots around 2031 could take our cutter shifts before I can replace the wage. Written staffing dates, a funded paid safe tooling place accepted by a nearby employer, and actual job ads with enough base pay after travel would help. I would not leave the line for a course title alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether the night crew gets the same practice machine as the day crew. A robot plan is not fair if only people who can train unpaid get the next job.

headlineQuote: A robot plan is not fair if only people who can train unpaid get the next job.
portrait: **Yusuf**, 58, is an experienced mid-level carton die-cutter operator with a vocational certificate and average machine skill.
He and his **partner Rina** have grown sons, lower operator pay, about three weeks' expenses saved and few similar factories nearby.
He uses **AI daily** for manuals and fault notes, likes early trials and supports union action for paid safe training.
Expected **2031 physical robots** could remove essential shifts; earlier retirement depends on written income covering real household costs.
biggestWorry: **2031 cutter robots** could erase his low-paid but necessary shift before a viable job or retirement income exists.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **written staffing dates**, accepted funded hands-on tooling training and posted safe local jobs with adequate base pay after travel.
